world_behind.title: Who Laban was
world_behind.text: The brothers size him up as a man who "can command fifty" (v. 31) — the language of a garrison officer, a captain of fifty in the old military reckoning (2 Kgs. 1; Isa. 3:3). He keeps the tribal records in his house, sits at the center of the city's power, and can order a killing without consequence. The plates were held by exactly the kind of man the coming judgment was aimed at.

cites.quote: can command fifty

spans.text: can command fifty

world_behind.title: Metal documents were treasure
world_behind.text: Engraving on brass was slow, skilled, expensive work reserved for what had to outlast paper and parchment. A compendium of scripture and genealogy on "plates of brass" (v. 3) was an archival treasure by any measure — which is why a fortune in gold and silver seemed, to the brothers, a plausible price for it.

cites.quote: plates of brass

spans.text: plates of brass

world_behind.title: The road they kept re-walking
world_behind.text: The errand means retracing the whole flight of chapter 2, up from the Red Sea camp to Jerusalem, with a side journey down to the abandoned estate and back. The chapter's misery is partly physical: hundreds of miles walked toward the danger their father was commanded to flee.

world_behind.title: Lots were referral, not gambling
world_behind.text: Casting lots was an accepted way of handing a decision upward when merits could not settle it (Prov. 16:33); priestly duty rosters ran on it. The brothers begin with a socially normal, even pious, procedure — which is part of the chapter's quiet argument about the difference between procedure and revelation.

world_behind.title: An estate with no protection
world_behind.text: The family's wealth sat on "the land of our father's inheritance" (v. 16) outside the city — retrievable, portable, and utterly unprotected once its owner had fled. Laban's seizure of it (v. 25–26) was confiscation by a man with soldiers, against which a fugitive family had no recourse at all.

cites.quote: the land of our father's inheritance

spans.text: the land of our father's inheritance

world_behind.title: The oath that binds a company
world_behind.text: "As the Lord liveth, and as we live" (v. 15) is the era's strongest form of binding speech — an oath on God's life and their own. Once sworn, abandoning the errand would make the speaker a false swearer before heaven. The brothers' persistence after two failures rests partly on that sentence.

cites.quote: As the Lord liveth, and as we live

spans.text: As the Lord liveth, and as we live

words.text: The company's first method: "we cast lots" (v. 11) at the door of the problem. It is decision by referral, respectable and scriptural, and the record does not mock it — but the lot picks the eldest, the eldest tries conversation, and conversation fails. The chapter is arranged so that ordinary procedure gets the first turn and cannot finish the errand.

cites.quote: we cast lots

spans.text: we cast lots

words.text: Laban's legal word does his violence for him: name the visitor "a robber" (v. 13) and the killing becomes lawful. Twelve verses later it is Laban who takes property by armed threat. The record lets the accusation curdle into description without a word of comment.

cites.quote: a robber

spans.text: a robber

words.text: When Laban saw the wealth, "he did lust after it" (v. 25) — the flesh-word, not a commerce word. The choice of verb files his crime under appetite rather than negotiation, and it quietly grades him: the man guarding the words of the prophets is governed by wanting.

cites.quote: he did lust after it

spans.text: he did lust after it

words.text: The family's shelter has been shrinking all book: a house in Jerusalem, a tent in the valley, now "the cavity of a rock" (v. 27). The concrete little word marks the bottom of the descent — and it is in the hole in the rock, not the house or the tent, that an angel first appears to this family's sons.

cites.quote: the cavity of a rock

spans.text: the cavity of a rock

words.text: The rod lands on the younger brothers, and the angel arrives mid-stroke: "as they smote us with a rod" (v. 29). Within a chapter the same verb will be handed to Nephi with Laban under it. The record tracks who smites whom, and why, with an accountant's care — the word is one of its scales of judgment.

cites.quote: as they smote us with a rod

spans.text: as they smote us with a rod

phrases.text: The object that will anchor the civilization is named for the first time in the record here, in Lehi's dream-commission. Everything about the volume's later shape — its quotations of Isaiah, its preserved Hebrew genealogies, its sense that scripture is a physical thing you carry — hangs on the errand this phrase sets in motion.

The murmurers' formula, quoted by Lehi before we ever hear the brothers say it. He answers the complaint by relocating the requirement: "I have not required it of them, but it is a commandment of the Lord" (v. 5). Hard is not denied; the address on the complaint is corrected.

cites.quote: I have not required it of them, but it is a commandment of the Lord

spans.text: I have not required it of them, but it is a commandment of the Lord

phrases.text: The answer-sentence: first person, future tense, two plain verbs, and a reason clause that carries the theology — "he shall prepare a way for them that they may accomplish the thing which he commandeth them" (v. 7). Nephi does not claim the thing is easy; he claims the way exists before the traveler sees it. Set against verse 5, the two grammars of the whole record face each other within three verses.

cites.quote: he shall prepare a way for them that they may accomplish the thing which he commandeth them

spans.text: he shall prepare a way for them that they may accomplish the thing which he commandeth them

phrases.text: The old oath formula of Israel's stories (1 Sam. 14:39), sworn by a young man in a hiding place. Nephi binds himself and his brothers to the errand with the strongest speech the culture has, and the narrative treats the oath as load enough to carry them through the next failure.

phrases.term: by the mouth of all the holy prophets
phrases.text: Nephi's phrase for why the records matter reappears, nearly word for word, in Zacharias's song and in Peter's temple sermon (Luke 1:70; Acts 3:21). Three speakers, three continents of time, one formula for prophetic continuity: God has one message and many mouths, and the plates are that message's shelf.

The angel speaks the old conquest register — the phrase Israel's war narratives use when God hands over an enemy — scaled to one household errand. The promise is left hanging over the chapter's end while the brothers do arithmetic against it, and the next chapter opens with Nephi carrying it like a key.

verses.label: v. 5–7
verses.title: Two answers to one command
verses.text: Lehi relays the commission honestly, including its cost, and the record stages the responses side by side: the brothers' "it is a hard thing" (v. 5) against Nephi's "I will go and do the things which the Lord hath commanded" (v. 7). Same command, same family, same road — the difference is entirely in the grammar each speaker chooses.

cites.quote: it is a hard thing

spans.text: it is a hard thing

cites.quote: I will go and do the things which the Lord hath commanded

spans.text: I will go and do the things which the Lord hath commanded

verses.label: v. 11
verses.title: The lot falls on Laman
verses.text: Chance selects the eldest, and the eldest does the reasonable thing: he goes in and talks. The attempt is neither foolish nor faithless — it is ordinary — and its failure starts the chapter's lesson that this errand will not be finished by ordinary means.

verses.label: v. 15–20
verses.title: The speech in the hiding place
verses.text: Nephi rebuilds his brothers' will with an oath and then an argument: the wealth below can buy the plates; the flight was commanded because the city "have rejected the words of the prophets" (v. 18); and the records exist to "preserve unto our children the language of our fathers" (v. 19) and the prophets' words with them. He persuades with purposes, not rank — the one authority a younger brother has.

cites.quote: have rejected the words of the prophets

spans.text: have rejected the words of the prophets

cites.quote: preserve unto our children the language of our fathers

spans.text: preserve unto our children the language of our fathers

verses.label: v. 24–26
verses.title: The fortune spent for nothing
verses.text: Attempt two is purchase, and it ends the family's wealth: Laban takes the gold and sends servants to kill the sellers. Everything left behind in chapter 2 is now truly gone — not renounced this time but robbed — and the chapter lets the loss stand without softening it.

verses.label: v. 27
verses.title: A hole in the rock
verses.text: The sons of a great house hide in "the cavity of a rock" (v. 27), propertyless and hunted. It is the book's lowest point so far, and the record's staging is deliberate: the angel comes to the cave, not to the camp or the city.

cites.quote: the cavity of a rock

spans.text: the cavity of a rock

verses.label: v. 28–29
verses.title: The rod and the question
verses.text: Failure turns inward as a beating, and heaven interrupts it mid-stroke with a question: "Why do ye smite your younger brother with a rod" (v. 29) The angel reaffirms the offensive promise — the younger will rule, "because of your iniquities" (v. 29) — and re-issues the errand with a guarantee attached.

cites.quote: Why do ye smite your younger brother with a rod

spans.text: Why do ye smite your younger brother with a rod

cites.quote: because of your iniquities

spans.text: because of your iniquities

verses.label: v. 31
verses.title: Murmuring survives the angel
verses.text: The chapter's last sound is the old voice, minutes after an angelic visitation: "How is it possible that the Lord will deliver Laban into our hands" (v. 31) The brothers do not deny the angel; they out-count him — Laban "can slay fifty" (v. 31). Sight, the record is already arguing, does not produce faith; it only changes what unbelief has to explain away.

cites.quote: How is it possible that the Lord will deliver Laban into our hands

spans.text: How is it possible that the Lord will deliver Laban into our hands

cites.quote: can slay fifty

spans.text: can slay fifty

chapter.title: Three attempts, in ascending order
chapter.text: The chapter runs asking (v. 11–14), then buying (v. 22–26), and holds its third method for the next chapter. The first two are the world's methods — protocol and purchase — and both fail against a man with soldiers. The structure is an argument about means: what the Lord commands, human competence alone will not finish.

chapter.title: The test passes to the next generation
chapter.text: Chapter 2 tested Lehi with leaving; this chapter tests his sons with going back. The road runs toward the danger this time, and the sons must obey a command relayed through their father rather than heard in vision — which is precisely the position most readers occupy.

chapter.title: What the record thinks records are worth
chapter.text: The chapter prices the plates in the only currencies it has: a fortune in gold offered for them, and a stated purpose that reaches past every living member of the family (v. 19–20). The family trades its entire material inheritance, involuntarily, for its textual one — and the record never once suggests the exchange was a bad one.

chapter.title: Laban is the city in one man
chapter.text: Propertied, armed, seated in the center of things, guarding scripture he does not obey, calling the petitioner a robber while robbing him. The chapter gives Jerusalem's coming judgment a face, and the face is respectable.

chapter.title: The angel changes the situation, not the hearts
chapter.text: Verses 29–31 stage a controlled experiment the book will repeat for a thousand years: an unambiguous heavenly messenger, and within moments, fresh murmuring. The brothers' unbelief is not evidence-starved; it is a settled way of counting, and the chapter lets the reader watch it survive an angel.

chapter.title: Middle panel of the departure unit
chapter.text: The unit's two return journeys give it its shape: this one for the record, chapter 7's for the families. A covenant colony, the structure says, needs scripture and seed both — and the scripture came first.

chapter.title: A narrator honest about his house
chapter.text: Nephi preserves the beating, the hard words, and his brothers' names attached to both; he also preserves Lehi's careful honesty ("I have not required it of them" (v. 5)) and his own self-assurance. The family record keeps the family's shame, which is one of the stronger reasons to trust it elsewhere.

cites.quote: I have not required it of them

spans.text: I have not required it of them

applications.title: Trade grammars
applications.text: The difference between the brothers and Nephi in this chapter is a sentence-shape: "it is a hard thing" against "I will go and do." Pick the commanded thing you currently narrate in the hard-thing grammar and re-say it, out loud, in the going grammar. The sentence will not do the errand, but it decides who is driving.

applications.title: Hunt for the prepared way
applications.text: Nephi's claim is not that commands are easy but that ways are prepared. For one current assignment, inventory what has already been laid down — the person you already know, the skill you already have, the timing that already broke your way — and treat the inventory as the way appearing.

applications.title: Bind yourself first, then persuade
applications.text: Nephi leads his reluctant brothers by taking the oath himself before asking anything of them, then arguing from purposes that outlast the night. When you need to move unwilling people, commit yourself visibly first, and give them reasons that will still be true in a year.

applications.title: Audit the price you'll pay for scripture
applications.text: The family spent its whole fortune, without hesitation, to get the word of God into its children's future. Set that against what access to scripture costs you now — minutes, mostly — and let the imbalance set this week's reading.

applications.title: Spend the miracle before it cools
applications.text: Between the angel's departure and the murmuring's return there was a gap of minutes. When an undeniable spiritual moment comes, write it down and obey it in some concrete way the same day — the arithmetic voice is already warming up.

applications.title: Watch the fifty-math
applications.text: The brothers' unbelief is precise: fifty against four. Faith's arithmetic in this chapter starts from a different first term. Name the "fifty" you are currently counting, and then name what you are leaving out of the count.

questions.text: When a hard assignment reaches me through someone I can argue with, do I answer the messenger or the Sender?
What way was prepared for me the last time I obeyed something difficult, and did I recognize it at the time or only after?
Which decisions in my life am I settling by lot — habit, default, whoever speaks first — that deserve actual asking?
What would I go back for, at real risk, if I had to choose what my children inherit from me?
Which words of the prophets am I actively preserving for the people who come after me, and in what form will they find them?
When my plans fail, who is nearest to my rod — and what does my family's record of this year preserve about me?
Which past moments of unmistakable help has my own fifty-math already explained away?
